title: Clarifying a design brief for a small business
scenario: A freelance graphic designer receives a vague brief from a local bakery about logo ideas. The owner wants a design that feels warm and inviting but hasn’t specified fonts, colors, or constraints. The conversation must refine their vision without leading them to unrealistic expectations.
user_persona: A practical, detail-oriented freelance designer who enjoys baking but prefers clear directions. They enjoy sharing personal baking anecdotes to build rapport and mention they’re currently working on a small studio setup.
assistant_mode: Professional collaborator with technical precision. Asks structured questions to uncover unspoken needs, offers hypotheticals, and corrects assumptions without judgment. Avoids jargon or subjective praise.
goal: Extract key design constraints (e.g., color palette, imagery, file formats) and potential timeline to provide a tailored proposal within the bakery’s budget.
resolution: The designer confirms the bakery’s brand colors (existing #1A3E2F and #D4A660), excludes human figures, and proposes a 2-week turnaround with one revision round, aligning with their studio’s workflow.
facts: The bakery’s current logo is a simple, hand-drawn illustration with muted greens and warm golds.
The owner mentions their sister owns a floral shop nearby, which uses pastels and intricate patterns.
The bakery’s primary products are sourdough bread and pastries, with a ‘farm-to-table’ focus.
The designer’s studio uses Figma for mockups and exports files in PNG/SVG for web/print.
Past orders show the designer works on 3-4 revisions per client and bills $750 for a logo suite.

title: Adjusting a book club’s discussion focus
scenario: A book club leader emails the group about *The House of the Scorpion*, but two members missed it. One is frustrated they’re behind; the other insists on discussing ‘symbolism’ first. The leader needs to refocus the discussion without alienating either member.
user_persona: A 30-year-old English teacher who loves dystopian themes but struggles with time management. They mention they’re currently teaching *1984* and joke about how ‘everyone’s a critic’ in their group.
assistant_mode: Supportive mediator with procedural expertise. Acknowledges emotions, offers structured alternatives, and gently redirects to shared goals. Uses humor sparingly to defuse tension.
goal: Guide the group to a mutually agreeable discussion plan (e.g., thematic vs. plot analysis) that aligns with their next meeting’s time constraints.
resolution: The group agrees to split their discussion: 20 minutes on symbolism (e.g., Matty’s eyes) followed by a 10-minute plot recap for new members, using shared notes from the leader’s earlier email.
facts: The book club meets monthly for 1.5 hours via Zoom, with a mix of new and returning members.
The leader’s previous meetings alternated between thematic analysis and Q&A with the narrator’s perspective.
One member (Alex) emailed last week asking for ‘chapter summaries’ to catch up, while another (Jamie) posted on the group chat: ‘Symbolism is my jam—let’s dive in!’
The leader’s notes include 3 key themes: oppression, identity, and nature vs. technology.
Alex’s schedule shows they’re free for a 2-hour session but not the usual 1.5-hour slot.

title: Resolving a gift exchange deadline conflict
scenario: A friend’s holiday gift exchange is three days late, and two participants (a family friend and a coworker) are already done exchanging. Your friend asks for advice on how to proceed without causing awkwardness, as they’re short on time but don’t want to ‘cheat.’
user_persona: A 28-year-old event planner who’s organized 10+ gift exchanges but hates last-minute scrambling. They mention they’re currently planning a birthday party and joke, ‘I should’ve known December would ruin me.’
assistant_mode: Pragmatic strategist with social awareness. Provides options without moralizing, cites real-world precedents, and helps weigh trade-offs (e.g., time vs. effort). Uses dry humor to soften suggestions.
goal: Help your friend propose a solution that maintains group harmony while acknowledging the deadline slip, ideally without rewriting the exchange’s rules.
resolution: Your friend suggests a ‘virtual catch-up’ with the two who’ve already exchanged—offering a handmade coupon book (e.g., ‘One free babysitting hour’) as a non-monetary gift, paired with a heartfelt note explaining the delay. The group agrees it’s fair and less stressful than rewriting the exchange.
facts: The exchange typically involves 6-8 people, with gifts under $25 and wrapped the same night before sending.
The family friend lives 2 hours away and has already opened their gift (a hand-knitted scarf).
The coworker is a ‘last-minute shopper’ who bought a $20 gift card but hasn’t shared it yet.
Your friend’s current to-do list includes: ‘Buy 2x Christmas ornaments,’ ‘Send holiday cards,’ and ‘Plan coworker party,’ all due this week.
Past exchanges have included a ‘do-over’ rule if someone missed the date, but it was rarely used.

title: Volunteering time off work for a food drive
scenario: A part-time retail employee wants to volunteer for a food drive but must coordinate with their manager and the volunteer coordinator. They’re unsure how to phrase their time off request—especially with their shift schedule—and don’t want to overcommit. The food drive organizers need one volunteer for two hours on a weekend.
user_persona: 22-year-old retail associate in a non-union store, working 16/week, slightly anxious about asking for time off but wants to help their community. Values punctuality and respecting others’ schedules.
assistant_mode: Remote text helper for small, structured requests—provides templates, clarifies constraints, and ensures alignment between parties without taking sides. Uses neutral, professional language.
goal: The user will send their manager a clear, concise email requesting the time off with their food drive assignment confirmed, including shift coverage details, and feel confident the request is feasible.
resolution: The user’s manager approves the time off for the exact food drive slot, and the volunteer coordinator confirms the assignment. The user arranges for a coworker to cover their shift (15 mins of their own time) and receives written acknowledgment of all approvals before the event.
facts: The food drive is on Saturday, 10:00–12:00 AM at the city’s community center. The volunteer coordinator is Sarah, email: sarah@communityhub.org. She has pre-assigned roles and no backup volunteers.
The user’s manager, Jake, approves up to 4 hours of time off per quarter without penalty, but requires a coworker’s agreement to cover shifts and a 48-hour advance notice.
The user’s current weekly shifts are Wednesday 2–6 PM and Saturday 10 AM–2 PM. They have no other commitments on Saturday.
The food drive’s ‘assistant’ role (check-in/sign-in) requires no prior experience and is listed as ‘no prep, just show up.’
The user’s previous volunteer work was a one-time book fair, which went smoothly, and they mentioned this briefly to a coworker.
